title: Islam is built on five
hook: Islam is built on five: the testimony, prayer, zakat, Hajj and the fast
carry: built on five pillars, every one needed
tomorrow: before your first breath, what was already written down?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stranger in white asked questions he already knew, and an angel taught by quiz. He came to teach you your religion. Today, the shortest outline of it.
screen: `HE CAME TO TEACH YOU YOUR RELIGION.`

segments.voice: Somebody posts a song's lyrics with two lines swapped, and the comments go to war. Same words, same song. Does the order matter? Yesterday's question asked what holds the building of Islam up. Abdullah ibn Umar reports the answer from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: Islam is built on five. Testifying that there's no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger. Prayer. Zakat. Hajj. And the fast of Ramadan. Five pillars, and a building on top. Then, in Sahih Muslim, somebody swaps two lines.
screen: `TWO LINES SWAPPED.` → `ISLAM IS BUILT ON FIVE.` → `THEN SOMEBODY SWAPS TWO.`

segments.voice: A man repeats it back: Hajj, and the fast of Ramadan. Ibn Umar stops him. No: the fast of Ramadan, and Hajj. That's how I heard it from the Messenger of Allah. So, does the order matter? Here are two views, and each has a real case. The first is Ibn Umar's own. A report is a trust. The words came from the Prophet, so you carry them the way they came, order and all, because a small slip today is a different report tomorrow. The second: what you pass on is the meaning. Five pillars, none missing, and the building stands the same either way. Hadith scholars discussed reporting by meaning, and some allowed it for a careful narrator who knew the language well. Now the detail to tell a friend tonight. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the same hadith from Ibn Umar lists Hajj before the fast. Both orders sit in the sahih collections, and commentators have offered more than one way to fit them together. Under the argument, both sides agree on the picture: a building on five, and every pillar needed for it to stand. The debate is only about how carefully you carry the blueprint.
screen: `NO: THE FAST, THEN HAJJ.` · `VIEW ONE: CARRY IT AS IT CAME.` · `VIEW TWO: CARRY THE MEANING.` · `BUKHARI'S ORDER: HAJJ FIRST.` · then, large: `BUILT ON FIVE.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand. Fold down a finger for each pillar as you name it: the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast, Hajj. Then go back through them slowly, and for each one, let a face come to mind, someone you've seen pray, give, fast or travel for it, until the hand is closed.
screen: `ONE HAND, FIVE FINGERS.` · `A FACE FOR EACH PILLAR.`

segments.voice: Built on five: Islam pictured as a building on five pillars, the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast and Hajj, in whichever order they reached you.
Keep this one close: built on five pillars, every one needed, whichever order you heard them in. That's the third hadith, read.

howItsDone: Muslim children learn the five pillars among their first lessons, sometimes counting them on one hand, and some classes memorize this hadith in Arabic.

Abdullah ibn Umar.meaning: a companion of the Prophet, son of Umar, who reported this hadith

Hajj.meaning: the pilgrimage to Mecca, for those who are able

zakat.meaning: the yearly giving owed from wealth

Sahih Muslim.meaning: a major collection of hadith, gathered by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 16 (Islam built on five; the man who said 'Hajj and the fast', and Ibn Umar's correction)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): debate shape. The two views are (1) Ibn Umar's insistence on the order he heard (Sahih Muslim 16, the narration where a man says 'Hajj and the fast of Ramadan' and Ibn Umar answers 'No: the fast of Ramadan and Hajj; this is how I heard it from the Messenger of Allah'), and (2) the scholars' discussion of reporting by meaning (riwayah bil-ma'na), allowed by some for a narrator who knows the language well. Confirm the Muslim 16 sub-narration and that the summary of view two is fair.

Sahih al-Bukhari 8 lists 'al-hajj wa sawm Ramadan' (Hajj before the fast); al-Nawawi's Forty uses this order too. Confirm. The lesson says only that commentators have reconciled the two orders in more than one way (al-Nawawi's commentary on Muslim discusses it); no single explanation is given.
